content.text: Can't Cut List rule: A player on Yahoo's official Can't Cut List cannot be included in any trade that involves draft picks, unless both sides of the trade include a Can't Cut List player. Both players must be on the Can't Cut List at the time the trade is accepted — not just when it is proposed. Additionally, the number of Can't Cut players on each side of any such trade must be equal. For example, if Team A sends 2 Can't Cut players and picks, Team B must also send exactly 2 Can't Cut players back along with picks. You cannot send Justin Jefferson and a 2nd round pick for Gibbs, Amon-Ra, and a 1st round pick.

changelog.note: Can't Cut players could not be involved in any trade that included draft picks under any circumstances.

Rule updated: Can't Cut players CAN be traded in a deal involving picks, as long as BOTH sides of the trade include a Can't Cut List player at the time the trade is accepted. Example: Team A has Hopkins (Can't Cut) + 3rd round pick. Team B has Jefferson (Can't Cut) + 7th round pick. This trade is ALLOWED because both players are on the Can't Cut list at the time of acceptance. Trading a Can't Cut player for picks alone remains NOT allowed.
Clarification added: the number of Can't Cut players on each side of a trade must be equal. If one side sends 2 Can't Cut players, the other side must also send 2 Can't Cut players.

content.text: Each team keeps 2 players every year.

A player is kept for the round they were originally drafted or acquired, with a 2-round penalty applied each additional year they are kept by the same owner. Example: a player drafted in round 4 costs a 4th round pick in Year 1, a 2nd round pick in Year 2, and a 1st round pick in Year 3.

If a team does not have the exact round required for a keeper, the price becomes the next higher round available. Example: if a keeper is owed a 7th round pick but the team only has a 6th round pick available, the 6th round pick is used instead.
Players drafted in the top 2 rounds cannot be kept.
A player can only be kept by the same owner for a maximum of 3 years. After 3 years they must be released.
Free agent pickups can be kept for an 8th round pick.

If a player is traded, only the 3-year keeper counter resets to zero — the new owner starts fresh at Year 1. The keeper price and round bumps carry over fully to the new owner. Example: if a player was kept for a round 8 pick and was due to be kept with a round 6 pick the following year, those same rules still apply after a trade. The anti-rental rule also applies — if Team A trades a player to Team B, Team A cannot receive that player back directly from Team B. The player must pass through at least one additional team (Team C) before returning to Team A.
Keepers must be submitted before the deadline. If not submitted in time, the commissioner will select the 2 highest ranked players on the roster based on Yahoo Rankings.

content.text: Top 10 QB rule: In a SUPERFLEX league, QBs carry significantly more value than in standard formats. To reflect this, the top 10 QBs by Yahoo scoring rank are also subject to Can't Cut List trade rules — they cannot be traded for picks alone. If picks are involved in a trade with a top-10 QB, both sides must include a Can't Cut List player (or top-10 QB). If a player appears on both the Can't Cut List and the top-10 QB list, the overlap will not create an extra slot. Example: if Josh Allen is both on Yahoo's Can't Cut List and a top-10 QB, the list remains 10 QBs — the 11th ranked QB does not get added to fill his spot.

Timing: Yahoo's QB scoring rankings at the exact moment the trade is ACCEPTED determine whether a QB is in the top 10 — not when the trade is proposed or reviewed. Example: a QB ranked 11th plays Thursday Night Football and climbs to 10th. If the trade is accepted while he ranks 10th, Can't Cut rules apply. If by Monday morning he has dropped back to 11th and the trade is accepted then, he is no longer subject to those rules. The moment of ACCEPTANCE is final.

Standings are determined by a custom points system — not solely by win/loss record. Each week, two things are tracked independently: whether you won your matchup, and where your score ranked among all teams that week.
Win your matchup + score in the top 6 = 7 points
Win your matchup only (bottom half scorer) = 4 points
Score in the top 6 only (lost your matchup) = 3 points
Neither (lost and scored in the bottom half) = 0 points

The two point buckets are completely independent — your matchup result and your weekly scoring rank do not affect each other. A team that consistently scores well will accumulate points even through unlucky losses.
Standings are updated every Tuesday morning after weekly scores are finalized. Tiebreaker: total points scored on the season.

gl.note: Mr. Electricity opened with a league-high 235.40 in Week 1 and never looked back, going 3-0 with a league-best 552.90 points, 87 more than anyone else. Kenneth Walker III and Christian Watson led the charge, and the all-play record (27-6) says no one in the league was better.

Chupamela HPT went 4-0 and led the league with 621.40 points, winning by 18.1 a game on average. The closest call was an 8.25-point win over cuadz build 001 in Week 4, and Week 7's 172.65 was the second-best score of the week.

rb.note: Benchwarmers finished no lower than 3rd in league scoring any week (207.88, 182.78, 179.10) and went 3-0 with a league-best 569.80 points, edging Hooligans by 10.6. Josh Allen scored 105.9 on his own, including 46.82 in Week 2, and the all-play record of 30-3 was the best in any league.

Hooligans went 4-0 with a league-best 772.64 points, 42.8 more than anyone. Week 5 was a 0.20-point escape (214.14 to 213.94), and Week 7 was a 70.60-point blowout. Cris's K-9 Unit also went 4-0 but scored 154 fewer points.

bh.note: The only unbeaten team in Beaners & Hussein. Love Thy Nabers never led the league in scoring, but won every matchup (144.55-132.10, 143.75-134.50, 129.60-101.25) with Dak Prescott and Trey McBride doing the work. It’s a record-first win: the points ranked 7th, and The Bijan Era was close behind.

An Underdog Story went 4-0 against opponents averaging 137.7 points a game, compared with 131.2 for Cris. Gio scored 613.20 (2nd in the league), led by Josh Allen, Jaylen Warren and Jonathan Taylor. Cris scored more (668.85) but lost in Week 4, so the perfect record and tougher schedule gave Gio the edge.

sts.note: I Like Tets won every week and finished in the top 6 in scoring every week, taking all 21 of the 21 possible points in the STS scoring system. Derrick Henry and Brock Purdy (42.25 in Week 3) drove a month that was as steady as it was good.

Youngbossbrian led Shoot the Shits with 677.75 points and a 36-8 all-play record. Brian had the top score in Weeks 4 and 5 (172.55 and 213.20), and the only loss came in Week 6 (123.65 to 152.30). No team in STS went 4-0 this month.
